question: A 40-year-old man is brought in after a crush injury. He has a pelvic fracture with a laceration communicating through the perineum into the rectum. Which single intervention, if omitted, carries the greatest risk of sepsis-related mortality in this open pelvic fracture?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A Foley catheter (or suprapubic catheter if urethral injury is suspected) is important for monitoring output but does not address the primary source of septic contamination — ongoing faecal contamination from the rectal wound.

Diverting colostomy is the single most mortality-reducing intervention in open pelvic fractures communicating with the rectum. Without faecal diversion, ongoing rectal contamination drives sepsis and pelvic osteomyelitis, which are the leading causes of late mortality. This must be done as part of early damage-control surgery.
External fixation is important for early mechanical stabilisation but, without faecal diversion, the contaminated pelvic cavity will cause sepsis regardless of how well the fracture is stabilised.

Distal rectal washout (irrigation of the distal bowel segment) is performed alongside colostomy to clear residual stool from the defunctioned segment — it is an adjunct, not the definitive intervention. Colostomy is the primary step.

overallFeedback.feedback: In open pelvic fractures with rectal communication, faecal contamination is the driver of septic mortality. Diverting colostomy is the intervention that interrupts this pathway. Review the surgical priorities for open pelvic fractures (Maheshwari Chapter on pelvic injuries).

Correct. The mortality of open pelvic fractures exceeds 50% if faecal diversion is not performed. The full damage-control sequence is: haemorrhage control → wound debridement → colostomy + distal washout → fracture stabilisation.
